## Introduction

Resistance training (RT) is the most effective strategy to counteract age-related declines in muscle mass and strength [@fragala_resistance_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016], and older adults are expected to benefit provided the anabolic stimulus is sufficient [@chen_is_2023; @paulussen_anabolic_2021], with training volume a principal determinant [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017]. This paper asks whether the molecular response to RT differs with age and dose, while a companion paper [REF]<!-- how to ref this, it wont be published --> addresses how much older adults gain in muscle size and function relative to young.  

Whether the anabolic stimulus is sufficient may depend in part on how responsive ageing skeletal muscle is to it. Earlier findings suggest that older adults have less responsive skeletal muscle, with a lower muscle protein synthesis (MPS) response to a single RT session or protein ingestion [@atherton_muscle_2012; @timmons_molecular_2016; @wall_aging_2015]. However, baseline MPS does not differ by age, and MPS-influencing proteins (e.g., mTOR) are more active in fasted muscle from older adults [@hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016; @markofski_effect_2015]. This may reflect compensation for increased relative muscle loading or dysregulation of the mTOR complex [@timmons_molecular_2016]. Ribosomal gene transcription and ribosome biogenesis are also reduced in older adults [@chaillou_does_2023; @hodson_molecular_2019; @timmons_molecular_2016]. The increase in ribosomal content with RT is believed to support fibre hypertrophy by increasing translational capacity [@figueiredo_regulation_2019; @figueiredo_revisiting_2019], and, individuals who respond to RT accumulate markers of ribosome biogenesis (e.g., total RNA and/or rRNA) compared to those who do not, regardless of age [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @stec_ribosome_2016; @stec_effects_2015].

The companion paper separates age differences in the response to RT into differences in capacity, in sensitivity to the training dose, and in the time taken to respond [REF]. Applied to ribosome biogenesis, we ask whether older muscle reaches a lower level of translational capacity, needs more training volume to reach the same level, or reaches it later. Training volume is a natural lever for sensitivity, supported by the dose-response relationship in younger adults [@schoenfeld_dose-response_2017] and by recent findings that older "non-responders" improved hypertrophy with higher volume [@lixandrao_higher_2024]. In contrast, a halfway-point measurement speaks to the time course. In young adults, total RNA rises within the first weeks and then plateaus or declines [@hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @brook_synchronous_2016], whereas the time course in older adults is less clear, with no change at 3 or 6 weeks in one study [@brook_synchronous_2016] and increases in responders after 4 weeks in another [@stec_ribosome_2016]. Repeated biopsies from the same muscle may alter gene expression in later samples [@friedmann-bette_similar_2012; @van_thienen_biochemical_2014; @long_short-term_2023], so an older non-training control group was included for total RNA and the protein markers to separate effects of training from those of the sampling. The present study aimed to determine how markers of ribosome biogenesis (total RNA, UBF and c-Myc) and the transcriptome respond to low- and moderate-volume RT in young and older adults.

### Study Overview

This study was an age-stratified, within-participant trial using a unilateral design. All participants performed a whole-body unilateral training program, with low- and moderate-volume protocols randomly assigned to either leg/arm. The intervention lasted 12 weeks, comprising 10 weeks of training and two weeks of testing (@fig-study-design). Participants completed 24 training sessions: two per week for the first five weeks, three per week for the following four weeks, and a taper to two sessions in the tenth and final week. Muscle biopsies were sampled at baseline, after three weeks of training (six sessions) and post-intervention. Effects of the intervention on muscle mass, strength and glucose tolerance are reported separately [@COMPANION]. Biopsies were sampled at the same time of day (± 2 h) in an overnight fasted state. Participants were asked to maintain their habitual physical activity level throughout the intervention and not to perform any additional heavy exercise. All participants gave their written informed consent before study enrollment. The study was approved by the Regional Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics - South-East Norway (ID nr. 255224), pre-registered at clinicaltrials.gov (Identifier: NCT05063279), and conducted according to the Helsinki Declaration. 


### Participants

Thirty-two young (24 ± 3.1 years) and 49 old (75.5 ± 5.6 years) adults were recruited locally; 10 of the old participants were randomly allocated to a control group. Inclusion criteria were age 20–30 or > 70 years (@fig-study-design). Exclusion criteria were: insufficient Norwegian proficiency; RT more than once weekly and/or endurance training three or more times weekly within the last six months; unstable cardiovascular disease; illness or injury contraindicating RT; serious mental illness; or allergy to local anaesthesia.


### Resistance training protocol

The resistance training was a whole-body program with six unilateral exercises: three lower-body (leg press, knee extension, and knee flexion) and three upper-body (chest press, bent-over rows, and bicep curls), using individualised settings on all apparatuses. The low-volume condition consisted of one set of 10RM per exercise, whereas the moderate-volume condition consisted of three sets of 10RM per exercise, creating a clear contrast between conditions. Participants cycled on an indoor exercise bicycle for 5-10 minutes as a general warm-up. Before lower-body exercises, participants performed 1 set of 10 repetitions on the bilateral leg press (~50% of exercise load), and before upper-body exercises, they performed a warm-up set of 10 push-ups, modified to their individual fitness level (e.g., standard, from the knees, or against a wall). To ensure progressive loading and adequate skeletal muscle stimulation, the exercise load increased in the following set if participants completed more than 12 repetitions. Resting time between sets was two minutes. Trained personnel monitored all sessions for safety and standardisation. Training days were separated by at least one day throughout the intervention to ensure sufficient recovery.


### Skeletal muscle sampling and analyses

Muscle biopsies were collected from m. vastus lateralis. The biopsies were sampled under antiseptic and anaesthetised conditions (Lidocaine 10 mg ml-1, Mylan Hospital AS, Oslo Norway), using the micro-biopsy technique with a 12-14 gauge needle (Universal Plus, Mermaid medical A/S, Stenløse, Denmark) operated with a spring loaded biopsy gun (Bard Magnum, Bard Norway A/S, Oslo, Norway). Samples were divided into aliquots for RNA and protein analyses. At weeks 3 and 12, 48 hours separated the previous training session and biopsy sampling. 


### Protein extraction and western blotting

```{r}
library(dplyr)

# Participants and samples that entered a brms model.
# Age group and allocation are joined from reliefdata, so the function
# works regardless of how each model coded its groups (tx / tx_sex).
model_n <- function(fit,
                    id = "participant",
                    sample_vars = c("participant", "time", "leg")) {
  d <- fit$data |>
    mutate(participant = as.character(.data[[id]]))
  
  groups <- reliefdata::relief_participants |>
    mutate(participant = as.character(participant),
           age_grp = if_else(age < 40, "young", "old")) |>
    distinct(participant, age_grp, allocation)
  
  overall <- tibble(
    participants = n_distinct(d$participant),
    samples = nrow(distinct(d[, sample_vars])),
    rows = nrow(d)   # technical replicates for total RNA
  )
  
  by_group <- d |>
    left_join(groups, by = "participant") |>
    summarise(.by = c(age_grp, allocation),
              participants = n_distinct(participant),
              samples = nrow(distinct(pick(all_of(sample_vars))))) |>
    arrange(age_grp, allocation)
  
  list(overall = overall, by_group = by_group)
}

names(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mhi2.post.rds")$data)

n_rna  <- model_n(readRDS("fits/01-total-rna/m4.post.rds"))
n_ubf  <- model_n(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mu2.post.rds"))
n_cmyc <- model_n(readRDS("fits/02-protein/mhi2.post.rds"))


```


The wet muscle tissue from `r n_ubf$overall$samples` samples was freeze-dried for 24 hours and dissected, then homogenised with a plastic rod in ice-cold lysis buffer. Briefly, 150 µL of RIPA buffer was added per mg of muscle tissue dry weight, with 1 µL protease/phosphatase inhibitors per 100 µL lysis buffer. Samples were kept on ice at all times except when manually disrupting to homogenise the tissue, then incubated for 30 min on a rotator while on ice. After incubation, samples were centrifuge for 40 minutes at 15,000g at 4°C. Total protein was then diluted to a 2 µg/µL stock and aliquoted in triplicate for protein concentration determination and western blotting. Protein concentration was determined in a 1:10 dilution (Pierce Detergent Compatible Bradford Assay Reagent, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Oslo, Norway).

Western blots were performed using the Jess Automated Western Blot System (Bio-Techne, Minneapolis, USA), following the manufacturer's protocol, optimised for our lab. The stock solution (2 µg/µL) was prepared with fluorescent master mix from the EZ standard pack (Bio-Techne) and 0.1X sample buffer (Bio-Techne) and thus diluted to 0.75 µg/µL for the assay. The assay samples were then briefly vortexed, denatured at 95°C, vortexed and spun down prior to loading the assay plate. To control for within-plate variation, we used a total protein normalisation reagent (Bio-Techne) for all assays. A specific between-plate normalisation was not used; however, all samples from one participant were analysed on the same plate. Primary antibodies were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Texas, USA): UBF 1:50, UBF F-9, sc-13125; and Cell Signalling Technology (Massachusetts, USA): c-Myc 1:15, c-Myc D84C12. Ready-to-use secondary antibodies (anti-mouse and anti-rabbit) were purchased from Bio-Techne. After loading, the assay plate was centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 5 min at room temperature. The assay was then run on the Jess system with the chemiluminescence detection module.

### Total RNA extraction and RNA sequencing

Total RNA was extracted from `r n_rna$overall$samples` samples of muscle tissue, homogenised using TRIzol, 0.5mm RNase-free Zirconium beads (\~50 ul; Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA) and mechanical agitation (Bullet Blender, Next Advanced, Averill Park, NY, USA). Chloroform (Sigma-Aldrich, Oslo, Norway) was used for phase separation, and the RNA pellet was precipitated with isopropanol (VWR International, Oslo, Norway). For assessment of RNA content and purity, RNA was eluted in TE buffer (1:2) and assessed via spectrophotometry. Samples with a 260/280 ratio below 1.8 were excluded. The RNA stock was stored at -80°C until further analysis.



`r nsamp` total RNA samples were selected for RNA-sequencing analysis; `r nsamp_included` samples passed the initial quality assessment (RIN > 8) and were used in downstream analyses. The samples were selected from the pool of intervention participants that had both baseline and post samples collected. Purified mRNA (poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads) was used for library preparation and subsequent 150-bp paired-end sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq, Novogene Europe, Cambridge, United Kingdom). Raw reads were filtered (SOFTWARE, settings) and aligned to the Human genome (Release), followed by gene- and transcript-level quantification using RSEM (version).

Gene counts (filtered for low-abundance targets) were modelled using a regularised negative binomial generalised linear mixed model [@glmmmtb] including model parameters for sex, time (baseline and post-intervention), age-group (young and old) and condition (low- and moderate-volume) and the interaction between time, age and condition. A varying intercept (random effect) was used for participant, and the dispersion parameter was estimated using the `nbinom2` parameterisation available in `glmmTMB`[@glmmmtb]. The effective library size [@robinson2010;@edger] was included as an offset to account for sequencing depth. Regularisation through an empirical Bayes shrinkage approach[@efron2010] was achieved using a two-step approach. First, naive models were fitted for all target counts (gene/transcript) using our in-house pipeline [@seqwrap] and estimates for all model parameters (except the intercept) were used to create priors for subsequent informed models. Fixed-effect priors were constructed using a normal distribution with mean and standard deviations from each parameter value from the first model pass; the prior for the varying intercepts was constructed using a gamma distribution with the shape parameter informed by the mean from the naive model estimates and the scale parameter fixed to 2. Finally, the dispersion parameter priors were constructed by fitting a trend model (Local Polynomial Regression Fit) to the association between raw mean log counts and log dispersion across all targets. The predicted dispersion at the target-specific raw mean log count was used as the mean, and the model residual standard error was used as the standard deviation to define a normally distributed target-specific prior.


### Statistical analyses

Total RNA yield was analysed on the log scale using a Bayesian multilevel regression (brms) fitted to the individual spectrophotometer wells, with a mean for each group-by-sex combination, time effects (baseline, week 3, post) within each, and log tissue mass as a covariate. Varying intercepts were included for participant (with a participant-specific time slope), leg and sample, so that well-to-well variation was separated from biological variation. UBF and c-Myc (high peak) were analysed in the same way, using peak area normalised to total protein, with varying intercepts for participant and leg and no time slope. Sensitivity analyses repeated the protein models without normalisation, after excluding low-quality capillaries, and with a plate intercept. The association between total RNA per mg tissue and UBF was examined descriptively with a mixed model. Contrasts were computed from the posterior draws at the population level, with the sexes, and the volume conditions where pooled, weighted equally, and are reported as percentage changes or differences in change (posterior mean, 95% credible interval; CI). P(>0) or P(<0), in the direction of the estimate, is given when the CI includes zero. Evidence was classified as credible (95% CI excludes zero), likely (≥ 90%), weak (75–90%) or no evidence (< 75%).

Gene-level RNA-seq counts (16,878 genes after expression filtering with edgeR) were analysed gene by gene with negative-binomial mixed models (glmmTMB, via seqwrap) containing sex, age group, a combined time-by-volume factor (baseline, post low volume, post moderate volume) and its interaction with age group, a participant-level varying intercept, and the log TMM-normalised library size as an offset. Parameters were regularised with empirical Bayes priors derived from a first, uninformed pass across all genes: normal priors for the fixed effects (mean and SD of the first-pass estimates), a gamma prior for the participant SD, and a prior on the dispersion centred on a loess trend of dispersion against mean expression. Contrasts were computed from model predictions (marginaleffects) with sexes weighted equally and tested with Wald tests, with p-values adjusted within each contrast (Benjamini–Hochberg; FDR < 5%). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (clusterProfiler; Gene Ontology biological processes, gene sets of 25–500 genes) was run on the contrast statistics, using BH-adjusted p < 0.01 and collapsing redundant terms with simplify (cutoff 0.5). Ribosome biogenesis was examined with a targeted enrichment analysis of eight a priori GO terms (including descendant terms; BH adjustment across these terms only) and with individual genes of the Pol I machinery and processing factors. To assess whether changes in these genes reflected biopsy composition, we compared the median change in ribosome biogenesis genes with that of myofibre-abundant genes (ACTA1, CKM, DES, MB, TNNT1, TNNT3, MYH1, MYH2, MYH7, TTN, NEB, MYBPC1, MYBPC2) and examined marker genes for non-myofibre cells (COL1A1, PDGFRA, PECAM1, VWF, PTPRC, PAX7). These composition analyses were descriptive.

## Results

### Exercise Volume Load

Total volume load was about 2.8 times higher with moderate than with low volume in both age groups (young: 137,439 ± 54,492 vs. 50,694 ± 25,708 kg; old: 118,125 ± 38,225 vs. 42,134 ± 14,353 kg).

### Protein

_UBF_
Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase UBF by week 3 (20.2%, 95% CI [−5.6%, 50.3%], P(>0) = 93.2%, @fig-protein-rna A), as did the control group (26.9%, 95% CI [−4.8%, 65.0%], P(>0) = 95.0%), with no evidence of a difference between them (−3.5%, 95% CI [−33.7%, 36.0%], P(<0) = 61.6%). Young adults also tended to increase UBF (17.2%, 95% CI [−6.6%, 44.2%], P(>0) = 91.6%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−1.1%, 95% CI [−29.0%, 34.8%], P(<0) = 56.0%). There was no evidence of an effect of training volume in young (3.9%, 95% CI [−34.0%, 56.6%], P(>0) = 52.4%) or older adults (−10.1%, 95% CI [−45.6%, 40.9%], P(<0) = 72.1%), or that the volume effect differed between age groups (22.4%, 95% CI [−39.3%, 117.1%], P(>0) = 68.1%; @tbl-protein-rna).

_c-Myc High Peak_
c-Myc (high peak, @fig-protein-rna B) decreased in the control group by week 3 (−35.6%, 95% CI [−55.2%, −9.9%]). Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) tended to increase c-Myc (26.6%, 95% CI [−6.4%, 66.5%], P(>0) = 93.7%), and their change was greater than that of the control group (103.1%, 95% CI [23.9%, 209.6%]; @tbl-protein-rna), a difference driven by the decrease in the control group. Young adults (averaged across volume conditions) showed weak evidence of an increase (19.4%, 95% CI [−9.7%, 54.7%], P(>0) = 88.8%), with no evidence of a difference from older adults (−3.6%, 95% CI [−35.9%, 39.9%], P(<0) = 61.4%). Within young adults, there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (3.9%, 95% CI [−29.1%, 47.1%], P(>0) = 54.0%), whereas moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (40.2%, 95% CI [−9.5%, 106.6%], P(>0) = 93.3%), with weak evidence of a difference between them (40.1%, 95% CI [−24.5%, 136.9%], P(>0) = 85.1%). In older adults, there was no evidence of a change with low-volume training (11.6%, 95% CI [−27.6%, 64.7%], P(>0) = 66.0%), whereas moderate-volume training tended to increase c-Myc (46.9%, 95% CI [−5.8%, 116.7%], P(>0) = 95.5%), again with weak evidence of a difference between them (37.7%, 95% CI [−27.6%, 137.8%], P(>0) = 81.8%). There was no evidence that the volume effect differed between age groups (11.6%, 95% CI [−55.0%, 135.2%], P(>0) = 51.7%).

### Total RNA

Older adults in the intervention group (averaged across volume conditions) increased total RNA by 11.7% at week 3 (95% CI [4.6%, 19.2%], @fig-protein-rna C) and by 15.5% at post (95% CI [6.5%, 24.9%]). The control group likely increased by a similar amount (week 3: 9.5%, 95% CI [−3.5%, 23.3%], P(>0) = 91.9%; post: 13.8%, 95% CI [−3.8%, 33.3%], P(>0) = 93.7%), with no evidence of a difference between the groups (week 3: 2.5%, 95% CI [−11.1%, 17.6%], P(>0) = 61.8%; post: 2.2%, 95% CI [−14.9%, 21.9%], P(>0) = 57.7%). Young adults increased by 19.6% at week 3 (95% CI [11.6%, 27.7%]) and by 13.1% at post (95% CI [3.9%, 22.6%]). All four intervention groups increased total RNA at both time points, with the 95% CI excluding zero in all but young adults with low volume at post (10.7%, 95% CI [−0.4%, 22.2%], P(>0) = 97.0%). Young likely had a larger early increase than older adults (7.2%, 95% CI [−2.6%, 17.6%], P(>0) = 92.1%), but there was no evidence of an age difference at post (−1.9%, 95% CI [−12.6%, 9.9%], P(<0) = 64.3%). Moderate volume likely produced a larger week 3 increase than low volume in young adults (8.6%, 95% CI [−3.5%, 22.2%], P(>0) = 90.8%), with weak evidence at post (4.8%, 95% CI [−7.5%, 18.6%], P(>0) = 76.0%), whereas there was no evidence of a volume effect in older adults (−1.0% at week 3 and 0.5% at post). There was weak evidence that the volume effect was larger in young than older adults at week 3 (10.1%, 95% CI [−7.1%, 29.8%], P(>0) = 86.0%), and no evidence at post (4.7%, 95% CI [−12.2%, 23.9%], P(>0) = 68.2%; @tbl-protein-rna). Lastly, there was weak evidence of a small positive association between total RNA and UBF, adjusted for time (0.08 SD per SD, 95% CI [−0.11, 0.26], P(>0) = 80.4%; @fig-protein-rna D).


```{r}
#| label: tbl-protein-rna
#| tbl-cap: "Total RNA (ng/mg tissue), UBF and c-Myc, high peak (corrected area): within-group changes and between-group contrasts. UBF and c-Myc were measured at baseline and week 3 (Pre-W3), total RNA also post-intervention (Pre-Post). Δ is the change in model-predicted values, with percent change from the back-transformed predictions. Between-group contrasts are the percent difference in change (ratio of within-group ratios − 1): intervention minus control, young minus older, and moderate minus low volume. A positive volume effect (Young vs. Old) indicates that moderate volume was more favourable relative to low volume in young than in older adults. Pooled estimates and contrasts average the low- and moderate-volume conditions with equal weight on the log scale, so a pooled percentage change is not the arithmetic mean of the two volume-specific percentages, and all estimates give the two sexes equal weight. Estimates are posterior means. Probability is the posterior probability in the direction of the estimate: credible, 95% CI excludes zero (P ≥ 97.5%); likely, P ≥ 90%; weak evidence, 75% ≤ P < 90%; no evidence, P < 75%."

readRDS("figures/tables/tab-rna-protein.rds")
```

### RNA-sequencing

_Baseline_

Comparing gene expression between age groups at baseline (young - old) revealed `r n_diff_expressed` genes with robust differences (FDR < 5%, Fig. [-@fig-rnaseq-baseline]A–B). Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis [@xu2024a] indicated relatively higher expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes in young participants, and relatively lower expression of genes related to immune activation (complement activation, classical pathway) and epigenetic regulation (heterochromatin formation).


```{r}
#| label: fig-rnaseq-baseline
#| fig-cap: "Baseline differences in gene expression between age groups. (A) Volcano plot of the baseline age contrast (Young − Old), showing the gene-level estimate (log₂ difference, adjusted for sex) against −log₂(FDR). The dashed line marks FDR = 5%, and positive estimates indicate higher expression in young. The ten most significant genes are labelled. (B) Rank-based gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the baseline age contrast for three representative Gene Ontology biological processes (oxidative phosphorylation, heterochromatin formation, complement activation, classical pathway). The upper panel shows the running enrichment score and the lower panel the ranked contrast statistic (z-score) across gene rank position, with genes ordered from higher in young (left) to higher in old (right). Coloured lines and bars mark the members of each gene set."
#| fig-width: 6.3
#| fig-height: 3.5


library(seqwrap)
m2r <- readRDS("data-out/m2-rnaseq.RDS")
m2s <- seqwrap_summarise(m2r, verbose = FALSE)

n_diff_expressed <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "ageyoung") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()



n_sig_young_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "young_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()

n_sig_old_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "old_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()

n_sig_old_volume_t3 <- m2s$summaries |> 
  dplyr::filter(term == "old_volume_t3") |> 
  dplyr::mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adj < 0.05) |> 
  nrow()


readRDS("figures/fig-rnaseq-baseline.RDS")

```

_Training effect_

Training induced a large, broad transcriptional response in both age groups: `r n_sig_young_t3` genes changed from baseline to post in young and `r n_sig_old_t3` in old participants (FDR < 5%). The strongest individual changes were in collagen and basement-membrane genes (e.g., COL4A1, COL4A2, LAMB1, PXDN in young; COL4A1, LAMA4, COL3A1, COL1A2, SPARC in old). Gene-set enrichment showed a similar response in both groups, with six of the top ten categories shared and with matching direction and comparable magnitude. Expression was higher for extracellular matrix and connective tissue remodelling (integrin-mediated signalling, cell adhesion mediated by integrin, collagen metabolic process) and lower for RNA processing and ribosome biogenesis (RNA splicing, mRNA transport, ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis). Only one gene showed an age-dependent training response (FDR < 5%; none at 1%), but enrichment analysis of the age x time interaction indicated modest differences in magnitude (Fig. [-@fig-rnaseq-training]A-B): the decrease in RNA splicing and related mRNA-processing categories was larger in young, as was the increase in angiogenesis and aerobic/cellular respiration categories. A smaller set of categories differed by age, with additional enrichment for cytoplasmic translation, mesenchymal cell migration and angiogenesis in young, and for coagulation- and vascular-related categories in old.

Because bulk biopsies contain more than muscle fibres, we asked whether the lower expression of these genes reflected a change in biopsy composition. The median change in ribosome biogenesis genes was small (-5.8% in young, -3.4% in old) and similar to that of myofibre-abundant transcripts (ACTA1, CKM, DES, MB and others; -5.7% and -9.2%), whereas markers of non-myofibre cells increased in both age groups (COL1A1 about +100%, PECAM1 about +30%, PTPRC +33-35%, PAX7 +15-19%). Genes of the Pol I initiation machinery and MYC did not change clearly. This pattern is most parsimoniously explained by a shift in tissue composition, in line with the higher extracellular matrix and angiogenesis signatures, and not by selective regulation of ribosome biogenesis.

The dashed line marks FDR = 5%, and positive estimates indicate a larger increase, or smaller decrease, in young. Only one gene exceeded FDR = 5%. _Training volume_

Moderate compared with low volume produced a detectable difference in old participants (`r n_sig_old_volume_t3` genes, FDR < 5%) but in only one gene in young participants. The formal age comparison of the volume effect was not significant, so the age difference should be regarded as suggestive. In old participants, higher volume was associated with relatively higher expression of mitochondrial and oxidative metabolism genes (inner mitochondrial membrane organisation, respiratory electron transport chain, purine-containing compound biosynthesis) and relatively lower expression of muscle contraction and translation genes (skeletal muscle contraction, cytoplasmic translation, muscle organ development, striated muscle cell differentiation, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). The effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, in both the number of genes and statistical strength. It was also accompanied by a further rise in the same non-myofibre markers (PTPRC +26%, PECAM1 +15%, COL1A1 +14%), so the lower expression of contractile and translation genes may partly reflect composition.  

## Discussion

<!-- Opening -->
The main finding was that total RNA, a marker of ribosome biogenesis, increased in all four intervention groups, but this increase in the old intervention could no be attributed to training because it also likely occurred in the old control group by a similar amount. In the old, there was no evidence of a difference between the intervention and control groups at either week 3 (2.5%) or post (2.2%). By post, the old and young reached similar levels by post (15.5% and 13.1%), with a likely larger increase in the young at week 3 (19.6% vs 11.7%), and moderate volume likely gave a larger early increase than low volume in the young, which had faded by post. UBF and c-Myc protein, measured at baseline and week 3 only, tended to increase in the trained groups. However, UBF increased just as much in the old control group, whereas c-Myc decreased in the control group and tended to increase with moderate-volume training. The RNA-sequencing data showed a large, predominantly age-independent training response, dominated by upregulation of ECM and collagen genes and downregulation of RNA-processing and ribosome biogenesis-related genes, which appears largely explained by a shift in biopsy composition. A volume effect on the transcriptome was observed only in the old, although the age difference was only suggestive.

<!-- Markers of ribosome biogenesis: old vs. young -->
Total RNA did not indicate a reduced ribosome biogenesis capacity in the old. The model-predicted baselines were similar in the two age groups (482 vs. 487 ng/mg); the old intervention group had increased by 15.5% at post, similar to the young (13.1%), and there was no evidence of an age difference at post (-1.9%). The time course differed somewhat. The young followed the expected early rise at week 3 (low = 14.9%, mod = 24.6%), as seen in previous data from our lab [@lian_glucose_2024; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @hammarstrom_benefits_2020], and the early increase was likely larger than in the old (7.2%), who had increased by 11.7% at week 3 (low = 12.5%, mod = 11.1%). From week 3 to post, the point estimates fell in the young (19.6% to 13.1%) and rose in the old (11.7% to 15.5%). An elevation above baseline with a downward trend, as seen in the young, is not surprising, as previous studies show an early rise after 2-3 weeks of RT onset, followed by a plateau or decline after several weeks of RT [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020; @hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @brook_synchronous_2016]. The pattern in the old is compatible with smaller or slower accumulation, but the early age difference was uncertain, and the difference at post was essentially null, so a delay is better seen as a possibility than as a finding. Taken together, the data do not support a blunted total RNA accumulation in the old, although they cannot show that the increase was definitively caused by the training. Acute rodent studies point the same way, although concentration rose later in the old in one of them [@haddad_aging-sensitive_2006; @west_normal_2019].

The increase in the old (11.7% at week 3 and 15.5% at post) contrasts with earlier studies, which found no change in the old after six weeks of unilateral training, while the young increased by 42% at three weeks [@brook_synchronous_2016], or small increases as seen in Lixandrao et al. (2025), with 7.5% after 10 weeks, non-significant [@lixandrao_molecular_2025], and in Stec et al. (2016), with 9% and 26% in the moderate and extreme responder clusters after four weeks [@stec_ribosome_2016]. Unlike Stec et al. [@stec_effects_2015], who found a 28% higher baseline total RNA in the old, the model-predicted baselines here were similar in the two age groups (482 vs. 487 ng/mg). Differences in biopsy timing, about 90 min after a session in Brook et al. (2016) and 48 hours in the present study, and in the training programs may have contributed. For instance, the present training program with six unilateral exercises for the lower extremities could be considered heavier than in Brook et al. and Lixandrao et al. [@brook_synchronous_2016; @lixandrao_molecular_2025]. This cannot be the whole explanation, however, since the young in Brook et al. (2016) trained identically and did respond. More importantly, because the old control group likely increased by a similar amount here, increases in studies without an untrained control, such as Stec et al. (2016) and Lixandrao et al. (2025), leave the cause of those increases uncertain.

<!-- Control group -->
Overall, the control comparison limits what can be concluded about training effects on total RNA in older adults. The old control group likely increased total RNA about as much as the old intervention groups, at both week 3 (9.5%) and at post (13.8%), though with less certainty. The intervention groups reached the credible threshold after both low and moderate volume at both time points, whereas this was also true for both volume conditions in the young at week three, and only after moderate volume in the young at post (low volume was likely). This difference in certainty mostly reflects precision rather than size: the control point estimates were similar to those of the pooled old intervention group (9.5% and 13.8% vs. 11.7% and 15.5%), but the intervals were about twice as wide, likely because the control groups was smaller than the old intervention group. The direct comparison showed no evidence of a difference between older adults in the intervention and control groups. Although post-strength testing occurred ~5 days prior to the biopsy, no strength testing occurred around the week 3 biopsy, when the control group had already started to increase, so an RNA spike from testing alone is an unlikely explanation. Total RNA is also a variable measure, and baseline total RNA has been found to correlate negatively with its own change [@godwin_relative_2024; @lundberg_early_2020]. The control group had a lower model-predicted baseline than the old intervention groups, which could contribute to regression toward the mean. Prior biopsies have been reported to alter gene expression and tissue characteristics in later samples from the same muscle when taken hours to a week apart [@friedmann-bette_similar_2012; @van_thienen_biochemical_2014; @long_short-term_2023], although not in all studies [@lundby_gene_2005]. Whether this extends to biopsies taken weeks apart, as here, is not clear. Finally, unrecorded factors such as season, physical activity or diet could contribute.

<!-- UBF and c-Myc -->
UBF and c-Myc protein, measured at baseline and week 3 only, followed the total RNA pattern in the trained groups. Overall, the main takeaway is that UBF changes appear largely time-related, whereas c-Myc shows a more training-specific response. UBF tended to increase in the old (20.2%) and young (17.2%) intervention groups, albeit weakly (low volume: young 17.0%, old 29.6%; moderate volume: young 18.9%, old 13.0%), but also in the old control group (26.9%), suggesting a general temporal effect rather than a training-specific response, as with total RNA. The c-Myc response was more training-specific: it fell in the old control group (-35.6%) and tended to increase after moderate-volume training in both age groups (young = 40.2%, old = 46.9%), with no evidence of an age difference. The c-Myc changes in the old groups also followed their baseline levels (moderate 3,686, low 5,104 and control 7,248 corrected area, with changes of +46.9%, +11.6% and -35.6%), so regression toward the mean cannot be excluded as a contributor to both the decrease in the control group and the large difference between the old intervention and control groups (103.1%, 95% CI [23.9%, 209.6%]). However, the observed changes in the trained groups do match previous short-term and acute findings [@figueiredo_impact_2016; @lian_glucose_2024]. Earlier human studies of older adults give a mixed picture. Stec et al. (2015) found no change in UBF or c-Myc 24 hours after a single session in either age group, but noted that short-lived responses may be missed at that time point. After the first session, Brook et al. (2016) found that c-Myc mRNA, c-Myc protein and TIF-1A rose in the young only, with biopsies taken about 90 min after the session, an acute window that the present study did not sample. After four weeks of training in older adults, c-Myc protein rose in all response clusters (+51% in non-responders, +250-357% in moderate and extreme responders), whereas UBF did not differ between clusters [@stec_ribosome_2016]. This is directionally consistent with the old intervention group in the present study, although without an untrained control group, a time effect cannot be ruled out. Total UBF protein has also been found to be a noisy measure, as in Figueiredo et al. [@Figueiredo_ribosome_2015], where total UBF was unchanged after eight weeks while phosphorylated UBF (Ser388) rose fivefold at rest, so the UBF result should be interpreted with caution. Total RNA and UBF were weakly and positively associated across samples (0.08 SD per SD, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.26], P(>0) = 80.4%), appearing weaker in the present study than the associations reported in earlier studies of young adults from our lab, where total RNA tracked UBF protein over the course of training [@hammarstrom_ribosome_2022; @lian_glucose_2024]. 

<!-- Ribosome biogenesis markers: low vs. moderate volume -->
As for training volume, only most a modest early association with total RNA. In the old, there was no evidence of a difference between low and moderate volume at either time point (week 3 = -1.0%, post = 0.5%). In the young, moderate volume likely gave a larger increase at week 3 (8.6%), with weak evidence at post (4.8%), and there was weak evidence at week 3 and no evidence at post that the volume effect differed between age groups (10.1% and 4.7%). The lack of a volume effect in older adults align with Lixandrao et al. (2025), who found no volume effect (1 vs 4 sets) on total RNA, c-Myc, or UBF in older adults after 10 weeks. The pattern in the young resembles Hammartsröm et al. [@hammarstrom_benefits_2020], who found 8.8% higher total RNA with three compared to one set after four sessions (week 2), which narrowed to 5.9% by week 12. The present week 3 estimate (8.6%) is close to their early estimate, and the smaller post estimate is in the same direction as their later one, fitting an early advantage of moderate volume that then wanes. Hammarström et al. [@hammarstrom_ribosome_2022] found no volume effect on total RNA in young, but this should be interpreted with care, since both legs performed the same volume in the first four sessions, when most of the rise occurred. Taken together with previous studies, it seems that volume does not have a lasting influence on total RNA accumulation, at least not at the volumes compared here. c-Myc was the only protein marker with some indication of a volume effect. At week 3, moderate volume tended to increase c-Myc in both the young (40.2%) and the old (46.9%), whereas low volume did not (young = 3.9%, old = 11.6%), with weak evidence of a larger increase under moderate volume in both age groups, and no evidence that this differed by age. The direction fits the higher c-Myc mRNA response to a moderate-volume session observed by Hammarström et al. (2020), although this was mRNA measured one hour after a session, and not resting protein. UBF showed no such pattern, with no evidence of a volume difference in either age group; if anything, there was a weak lean toward a larger increase with low volume in the old (-10.1% for moderate vs low). The c-Myc result shoul be interpreted with caution, as the intervals were wide and the evidence weak, and it was not accompanied by a difference in total RNA or UBF. Another complication is that ribosome-related transcripts do not necessarily increase with training. Brown et al. [@brown_low_2024] found no increase in ribosome-related gene expression after 10 weeks of RT in young adults, and legs with the largest gain in lean mass had lower baseline expression of most of the measured genes and a smaller change in expression following RT. They proposed that increases in translational capacity are acute and transient, followed by a refinement toward higher efficiency, which would make any volume effect on capacity markers hard to detect at later time points.

<!-- Transcriptome: age and training response - CONTINUE HERE -->
The RNA-seq pattern observed in the present study closely matches previous findings and is consistent with largely age-independent training response. An earlier metformin trial in older adults found that progressive resistance training increased expression of genes involved in ECM remodelling and down-regulated genes in RNA-processing pathways [@kulkarni_metformin_2020], the same two dominant, opposite-direction gene sets observed here. A recent reanalysis across training modalities in aged muscle likewise found that resistance training was mainly linked to ECM, collagen, adhesion and basement membrane genes, with negative enrichment of ribosome and spliceosome terms [@yang_transcriptomic_2026]. The main new finding is that the response was largely age-independent: 3,503 genes changed in the young and 4,241 in the old, 6 of the top 10 enriched categories were shared with matching direction and comparable magnitude, and only one individual gene showed an age-dependent response after FDR correction. Gene-set enrichment suggested that the old showed a smaller-magnitude version of the shared response, with less down-regulation of RNA splicing and less up-regulation of angiogenesis and aerobic respiration than the young. Whether this reflects the smaller early increase in total RNA in the old cannot be determined from the present data, and the RNA-seq data were analysed only from baseline to post, when total RNA was similar in the two age groups.

Baseline differences between age groups were marked (2,082 genes), with young showing relatively higher expression of oxidative phosphorylation genes and relatively lower expression of immune-activation (complement) and heterochromatin-formation genes. Lower mitochondrial gene expression in old muscle is a consistent finding at both the transcript level [@melov_resistance_2007] and the protein level [@deane_proteomic_2022], and Melov et al. (2007) also reported that 179 of 596 age-related genes shifted toward the young pattern after 26 weeks of resistance training. Kulkarni et al. [@kulkarni_metformin_2020] similarly found several age-related differences in RNA-processing genes were no longer present after training. The present data do not directly show such convergence, since the age-by-training interaction was essentially null at the single-gene level, but the enrichment results point in the same direction. The main implication is that the training response in ECM genes was clearly present in the old, even though age-related baseline differences remained. Impaired transcriptional responses in mitochondrial, ECM, and immune system genes have also been described as defining features of age-related anabolic resistance to resistance training [@deane_proteomic_2022], and the baseline differences here align with the first and last of these. The training response in ECM genes, on the other hand, was clearly present in the old. 

The down-regulation of RNA-processing and ribosome-biogenesis gene categories at post compared to baseline may at first glance seem inconsistent with the increased total RNA over the same period. However, the decline in ribosome-biogenesis genes (median -5.8% in young, -3.4% in old) was similar to that of myofibre-abundant transcripts (-5.7% and -9.2%), whereas markers of non-myofibre cells increased in both age groups, and genes of the Pol I initiation machinery and MYC did not change clearly. This pattern supports the main interpretation that the RNA-seq and total-RNA readouts are not directly contradictory, and it is compatible with a non-selective change, such as a shift in tissue composition in line with the higher ECM and angiogenesis signatures, but composition was inferred from marker genes in bulk RNA-seq without histology or cell-type data, so this remains an interpretation. Another reason that the two readouts are not contradictory is that the RNA-seq data are of poly-A selected mRNA, which says nothing directly about rRNA, which makes up the majority of total RNA [@haddad_aging-sensitive_2006; @stec_ribosome_2016]. A similar dissociation has been seen in other studies, where the 45S pre-rRNA fell while total RNA rose after 6-12 weeks of RT [@mobley_biomarkers_2018; @haun_pre-training_2019], and Brown et al. (2024) found no increase, or a decrease, in ribosome-related transcripts across 10 weeks. Mobley et al. (2018) proposed that this may reflect negative feedback, once translational capacity has been built up, which would be a possible reading of the present data if the composition shift did not account for the pattern. Because different molecules were measured, however, this should be seen as an analogy rather than evidence.

<!-- Transcriptome: training volume -->
Training volume affected transcriptome only in the old, but the age difference should be interpreted with caution. A substantial number of genes differed between moderate and low volume in the old (1,216 genes, FDR < 5%), whereas essentially no genes did in the young. Still, the formal age comparison of the volume effect was not significant. In the old, moderate volume was associated with relatively higher expression of mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism genes, and relatively lower expression of muscle contractile and translation genes (e.g., cytoplasmic translation, RNA splicing, mRNA processing, ribosomal small subunit biogenesis). The effect was considerably more modest than the main training effect, both in the number of genes and in statistical strength. The only comparable transcriptomic data in older adults are from Lixandrao et al. [@lixandrao_molecular_2025], who compared one and four sets of unilateral RT using RNA-seq in 9 older adults per responder group, and found no individual genes that differed between volume conditions. Using a latent-variable approach (PLIER), however, they found that medium responders had a lower immune, proteasome, and spliceosome content with four sets than with one, which is in line with the lower RNA splicing and mRNA processing categories at moderate volume in the present study's older participants. The number of participants in their analysis was far smaller than in the present study, which may explain why the gene-level result differed. 

An interesting feature of the present result is that higher volume was associated with lower expression of translation-related genes. At the same time, c-Myc tended to be higher at week 3 with moderate volume, and total RNA did not differ. The volume effect was also accompanied by a further rise in the same non-myofibre markers (PTPRC +26%, PECAM1 +15%, COL1A1 +14%), so the lower expression of contractile and translation genes may partly reflect composition, as for the main training effect. Brown et al. [@brown_low_2024] proposed that translational capacity rises acutely and transiently and is then refined, so that ribosome content can fall while efficiency rises (ribosome specialisation); a higher volume could plausibly speed up that transition. Notably, neither the transition nor translational efficiency was measured in the present study or Brown et al., so this remains speculative. Higher expression of mitochondrial genes with moderate volume could reflect a shift in training adaptation toward oxidative metabolism, and mitochondrial and ribosomal adaptations have been suggested to compete. However, a review of the literature concluded that little evidence supports such a trade-off [@mesquita_skeletal_2021]. Whether the volume effect in the old represents something meaningful for functional outcomes, such as the greater hypertrophy with moderate volume, cannot be determined from the present data. 

<!-- Strengths, limitations and conclusion -->
A strength of the present study is its inclusion of both young and older participants, an untrained older control group, and a within-participant comparison of volume conditions, which removes between-participant variation as an explanation for any volume effect. As of a recent review [@chaillou_does_2023], only two human studies had compared markers of ribosome biogenesis between young and older adults after resistance exercise, one after a single session [@stec_effects_2015] and one after six weeks of training [@brook_synchronous_2016], and we are not aware of studies combining this with a transcriptome-wide analysis and a volume manipulation. Severak limitations should be considered. First, the old control group was the only control group, and total RNA likely increased in it by about as much as in the trained old, although less certainly, so the increase in the old cannot be attributed to training, and a time or sampling effect in the young cannot be assessed. Second, the post-strength tests may not have been optimally timed relative to the biopsies. To reduce lab visits (due to COVID limitations initially), post-strength testing was done before the 22nd and 23rd RT sessions for the intervention group. Thus, the control group mirrored this design and had strength tests ~5 days before biopsies. This could, in theory, have influenced total RNA at post, but it cannot explain the rise at week 3, when there was no strength testing. Third, UBF and c-Myc protein were measured only at baseline and week 3 due to time constraints, so it is unknown whether the changes persisted, and the 48-hour interval to the last/preceding session means a residual acute response cannot be excluded. Fourth, the RNA-seq data were available only at baseline and post in the intervention groups, so transcriptional changes cannot be separated from effects of time or repeated sampling. Further, the RNA-seq data are poly(A)-selected mRNA and connot be used to assess rRNA; therefore, the comparison with total RNA is indirect. Fifth, total RNA is a proxy for ribosome content. It has previously been shown to be noisy: reported variation in total RNA change is large, and baseline total RNA has been found to correlate strongly and negatively with its own change [@godwin_relative_2024; @lundberg_early_2020], which makes small differences between groups hard to interpret. Sixth, many contrasts were uncertain, with intervals including zero, and the volume effects, in particular, are best viewed as weak evidence of direction. 

In conclusion, total RNA increased in the four intervention groups and likely also in the old non-training control group, with no evidence of a difference between the old groups, so the increase in the old cannot be attributed to training. The old reached a similar level as the young by post, with a smaller early increase, which does not support a blunted accumulation of total RNA in the old, and volume had at most a modest early influence in the young. UBF and c-Myc protein tended to increase in the trained groups, with c-Myc the more training-specific marker. The transcriptional response was dominated by ECM remodelling and a down-regulation of RNA processing genes, was largely age-independent, and appears largely explained by a shift in tissue composition. A volume effect on the transcriptome was seen in the old only, but this age difference is suggestive.
